newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE-Long haul ahead for Russia's fledgling stock exchanges.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Long haul ahead for Russia's fledgling stock exchanges.

text.p: Russia's fledgling exchanges, armed with some of the country's hottest and most liquid stock, are looking for a slice of the action in Russian equities, rated among the top performers in the world.

"The future is bright for stock exchanges in Russia," said Alexander Sarchev, deputy managing director of the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX), which recently began trading shares in four of Russia's biggest companies.

Share dealing here is dominated by the Russian Trading System (RTS), a computer-based stock quotation system used by brokers to trade by phone from their offices, which generates turnover of around $50-$100 million a day.
Exchanges, many of which initially traded goods such as cement and pyramid scheme vouchers while trying to attract trade in company shares, lost out to the broker-operated RTS in 1994.

But Sarchev says well-placed MICEX -- home of the domestic government securities market, Russia's largest market, with daily volume of $1 billion -- is now set to boost trade to 40 major names by the end of the year.
It currently trades four stocks -- international long-distance carrier Rostelekom, regional utility Mosenergo, metals producer Norilsk Nickel, and oil company LUKoil.

Until it added an afternoon session in July, MICEX shares trade volume was just $1-$3 million per two-hour daily session. Novosibirsk's Sibirskaya exchange has only about $1 million turnover in futures contracts.

While RTS has suspended dealing in shares of giant natural gas monopoly Gazprom which wants its stock traded only on "organised markets", Gazprom now trades on Moscow and St Petersburg stock exchanges and is preparing to trade on the Sibirskaya and Yekaterinburg exchanges.
Futures on the RTS index and some major stocks already trade on the St Petersburg Futures Exchange and the Moscow-based Russian Exchange.
"It's difficult to say how things will be in real life but there is the feeling that the regions are waking up and understanding what the market is," said Sarchev.
EXCHANGES OFFER SECURITY IN A RISKY MARKET
Exchanges are banking on their relative safety to attract clients, and analysts see their clearing and depositary services as an advantage in Russia's widely-dispersed, uneven market.
The RTS does not require deals to be registered and has no depositary-clearing system, so registering a deal can take days and fraud is a constant risk, some say.
"Deals worth millions of dollars are often not registered," said MICEX's Sarchev. "That kind of thing is not possible with us."
MICEX uses Russia's Uneximbank as its depositary and the MICEX Auditing Chamber to clear deals, Sarchev said, adding that all deals were settled and registered on the same day as the trade.

The Novosibirsk exchange says its deals are also settled on the day of the trade, while the St Petersburg Futures Exchange recently announced a state-of-the-art electronic depositary-clearing system to monitor deals as they take place.
The RTS and the market watchdogs, the Central Bank and the Federal Commission for the Securities Market, are all working on clearing systems, but promise no quick fixes.
"Developing a clearing system is a sophisticated question, so while they may be working on it, there is still a long way to go," said a trader at a Western brokerage.

The exchanges also offer a different kind of security. Traders say that while prices are comparable on the RTS, MICEX and Russian Exchange, since participants are the same in each, many use futures trading to hedge cash market deals.
EXCHANGES STILL TOO SMALL, RUSSIA STILL TOO BIG
But Western operators, still the driving force on Russia's emerging market, are uninspired by the exchanges' low volumes despite growing participation by domestic investors.

"An exchange far away in Samara or Smolensk won't be that popular for trading equities," said the Western brokerage trader. "It might be popular for municipal bonds, but it's unlikely that people will come to trade LUKoil or Mosenergo."
Not everyone is so pessimistic.

"The rebirth of Russia cannot happen just through Moscow," says MICEX's Sarchev. "It has got to go through the regions and foreign investors are already going to the regions where the main issuers are," he said, conceding that the process was nevertheless a long one.
Some say the exchanges are likely to stagnate until they see significant Western activity.
LEGISLATION REMAINS DISINCENTIVE TO WEST
More fundamentally, analysts say, the lack of full rouble convertibility and limits on the repatriation of profits still turn foreigners off the stock market.

Many major Moscow brokerages are registered offshore, and deals struck through the over-the-counter RTS electronic system are frequently settled in non-rouble currency through foreign accounts, analysts say.

"It's an offshore market and just having an exchange is not going to move it onshore," said CentreInvest research director James Fenkner, adding that tax policy on transactions must be clarified before dealers will be tempted to use exchanges in a big way.
Western players are also concerned about lax legislation on company disclosure requirements, analysts say.

"If there were normal tax conditions...and conditions for working on exchanges then Western clients would be glad to work on exchanges just as they work with government securities," said Yuri Agaronik, research director at brokerage Prospekt.
